stories.title: Hundreds hospitalised in Yangon cholera outbreak: Minister
stories.summary: Since Aug 9, 500 people have been hospitalised for diarrhoea, the key symptom of cholera.
article_sentences: 500 people in Yangon were hospitalised with severe diarrhoea, with 149 testing positive for cholera, according to the regional social affairs minister.
Myanmar's health system is struggling due to ongoing civil war and economic decline, worsening the cholera outbreak's impact.
Health authorities are conducting surveillance and control measures, with new cases declining after a peak of over 100 admissions on August 13.
A total of 500 people have been hospitalised for severe diarrhoea in Myanmar’s largest city, a Yangon official said on Aug 17, with nearly 150 testing positive for cholera.
Myanmar’s infrastructure and health sector are creaking after more than five years of civil war, in which more than 100,000 people are estimated to have been killed – and with the economy moribund.
Since Aug 9, 500 people have been hospitalised for diarrhoea, the key symptom of cholera, said the regional social affairs minister Bo Htay.
His comments were the first official confirmation that cholera was involved, more than a week after the first hospital admissions.
Rapid tests for cholera had shown 149 positive cases, he told the parliament for the Yangon region, which includes the country’s largest city.
Nine of them had been formally confirmed as vibrio cholerae cases by the National Health Laboratory, he added.
Cholera is a severe diarrhoeal infection caused by consuming contaminated food or water, and can be fatal within hours if not treated.
The World Health Organization describes it as “a global public health threat and indicates inequity and lack of social and economic development”.
More than 100 new patients were admitted to hospital on Aug 13, the minister said, but new cases had since declined.

stories.title: More hosepipe bans in force as drought declared - is your area affected?
stories.summary: Nearly three-quarters of England and all of Wales are under drought conditions, with repeated heatwaves leaving water supplies under strain. Both England and Wales provisionally recorded their driest July on record. This lack of rainfall - on top of hot, dry weather in spring and early summer - has begun to take its toll on rivers, crops and nature. Wessex Water has become the latest water provider to announce a hosepipe ban - the company's first for 50 years - taking the total number of people under such a measure to nearly 30 million. So how is your area doing and are you in a drought? There is no single definition of drought, but it is characterised by a period of low rainfall. As the ground dries out, crops and vegetation can begin to struggle. If dry conditions persist, rivers, reservoirs and groundwater levels can also fall, putting pressure on water supplies. Environmental bodies in each UK nation decide whether to declare drought or water scarcity by assessing current water resources alongside weather forecasts. Both drought and water scarcity can lead to hosepipe bans, if they are not already in place. While drought is driven by prolonged dry weather, water scarcity occurs when demand for water outstrips the available supply. This summer, restrictions have been introduced in some areas to help manage high demand.
